Hubert Humphrey was the thirty-eighth Vice President of the United States under Lyndon B. Johnson, serving from nineteen sixty-five to nineteen sixty-nine. A central figure in American liberalism, civil rights, and Cold War politics, Humphrey was known as "the Happy Warrior" for his relentless optimism and passionate speeches on civil rights, government activism, and American idealism. Before becoming Vice President, Humphrey served as a U.S. Senator from Minnesota and was a founding member of the Americans for Democratic Action, helping shape post-war liberal politics. He championed the Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four as a senator and later the Fair Housing Act of nineteen sixty-eight as Vice President. As Vice President, Humphrey served during the escalation of the Vietnam War. His initial support for Johnson's policies created tension with the party's emerging antiwar faction, which damaged his nineteen sixty-eight presidential campaign. He lost the nineteen sixty-eight election to Richard Nixon in one of the closest races in American history, hampered by his association with Vietnam and inner-party divisions. He attempted a political comeback with a second presidential run in nineteen seventy-two, finishing third in the Democratic primary behind Edmund Muskie and George McGovern. Humphrey returned to the Senate in nineteen seventy-one and remained an influential voice for progressive causes until his death in nineteen seventy-eight.
